newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Canada cuts rates to lowest in decades. [CORRECTED 19:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Canada cuts rates to lowest in decades. [CORRECTED 19:15 GMT]

text.p: The Bank of Canada on Monday cut its key bank rate to 3.50 percent from 3.75 percent, the lowest short-term interest rate level in Canada in 33 years.
Analysts said the move may not be the last of a recent series of rate cuts by the central bank, provided U.S. interest rates remain steady and the Canadian dollar continues to strengthen.
The central bank's rate reduction quickly prompted Canada's major chartered banks to lower their prime lending rates to 5.0 percent from 5.25 percent.
Prime rates in Canada are now at their lowest level since July 1956.
Financial markets responded positively with the Canadian dollar, Treasury bills and bonds all trading steady.

The Bank of Canada's bank rate is similar to the U.S. Federal Funds rate in that both rates are set by central banks and are viewed as market benchmarks. Canada's bank rate, which has changed in nature over past decades, is now at its lowest level since August 1963.

The latest rate reduction was the 10th cut this year and the 19th since Canada's central bank began easing in May 1995. The Bank of Canada has now cut rates by a total of 475 (corrects from 4.75) basis points since May 1995 in a bid to jump-start Canada's sluggish economy.
Analysts said Monday's cut was prompted by recent data showing Canada's economy continues to underperform in spite of the central bank's efforts.

"The seeds of it were set last week with the disappointing retail sales report and the pretty benign CPI report that we got," said Mark Chandler, senior economist with Goldman Sachs. "You see from the market reaction that it was largely anticipated."

Speculation that the central bank would again lower rates has circulated through the markets since October 21 after Canadian retail sales fell 0.4 percent in August. Retail sales had been forecast to rise by 0.4 percent.
Rate cut expectations grew the following day, after a report on the consumer price index for September confirmed inflation in Canada remains subdued at an annual rate of about 1.2 percent.
Canada's inflation rate, which is among the lowest in the industrial world, is now near the bottom of the Bank of Canada's 1.0-3.0 percent target band.

The cut was also prompted by recent strength in the Canadian dollar, analysts said. In a press release following the cut, the Bank of Canada cited the recent strengthening the Canadian dollar for its move.
Because a stronger currency makes Canadian exports less attractive, it is seen by the central bank as having a similar impact as a rate hike.

The Bank of Canada could cut interest rates even further this year provided the currency strengthens and the economy remains flat, predicted Jim Webber, vice-president of fixed-income research with TD Securities Inc.

However, many analysts expect the central bank to remain on hold until the next meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve on November 13. Dealers said the Bank of Canada is more likely to cut rates further this year if the Fed keeps U.S. rates steady.

"If the Fed doesn't go I think you can't rule out another move," said Michael Gregory, an economist and strategist with Lehman "If the market takes it in stride and gives the Bank of Canada another opportunity to ease I think they will."
